newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian farm coops warn of machinery shortages.
newsitem.headline: Serbian farm coops warn of machinery shortages.

text.p: Serbia's farm cooperatives warned on Tuesday the government's programme for exchanging commodities for farm machinery was behind plan as the harvest season approached.

"We will not get all the machines in time for harvest, and we cannot wait. Wheat is ripening, and in 15 or so days harvesting is over for us," Mirko Martinovic of PKB Korporacija, the biggest agricultural complex in Serbia, told a meeting in the Serbian Chamber of Commerce on Tuesday.
Machinery needed to arrive within five to six days, he said.
Little or nothing has been invested in agricultural equipment during the years of sanctions.
Like the rest of the economy, agricultural producers are burdened by a lack of cash or credits and an inability to collect payment for last year's crops.
To help the ailing sector, Serbia's Commodity Reserve Agency signed a deal with producers in late March to provide machinery and equipment in exchange for agricultural produce.

Under the deal, Idustrija masina i traktora (IMT), Industrija motora Rakovica (IMR), Zmaj of Zemun and Dvadestprvi maj (DMB) were to produce 176 million dinars of agricultural machinery and equipment within three months, including 2,200 tractors and 150 combines.
The agreement covers only this year's agricultural produce.
But machinery producers also complained of a lack of finance and an inability to obtain spare parts and components from equally cash-strapped sub-contractors.
"Harvest is on the threshold and I am afraid we will not be able to change much before it begins," said Milan Babovic of the Zmaj agricultural machinery plant.
Zmaj last year produced just 60 combines, of which 20 went to Macedonia, 20 to Yugoslav farms and 20 to trading firms in compensation deals.
"This just shows the situation buyers are in, and we are suffering the consequences as well," Babovic said.
"It looks like we will have to use existing machinery for some time yet. Buyers cannot afford to buy them and we cannot buy parts and components."
Cvijo Saric, a farm cooperative official, said if local firms could not supply machinery, the government should step in and allow imports.
"But it is too late to talk about this harvest now. We should talk about the 70 percent of harvesting that awaits us in the fall -- sunflower, maize, soybean," Saric said.
